canonical_statement: Colonists came to America seeking religious freedom, among other reasons.
linked_questions: The colonists came to America for many reasons. Name one.
curation_rationale: Most concrete and distinctive of the three; also the most culturally familiar version of this story (Pilgrims), giving the icon something specific to depict instead of an abstract 'freedom'.
visual_treatment: Paired with fact 77 as a 'why they came / why they revolted' contrast card — see cluster 'colonial_motivations'. Discovered mid-curation: these two facts were drafted separately as plain icon cards, then recognized as a natural contrast pair once both were curated. A cluster can upgrade two standalone facts into a joint technique after the fact, not just at planning time.

canonical_statement: American Indians (Native Americans) lived in America before Europeans arrived.
linked_questions: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
curation_rationale: Both accepted terms given together rather than picking one — this fact is about the people broadly, unlike fact 117 which asks for one specific tribe.
visual_treatment: Reuses the same respectful feather icon as fact 117, for visual consistency across facts about Indigenous peoples — plain, no gimmick.

canonical_statement: Africans (people from Africa) were taken and sold as slaves.
linked_questions: What group of people was taken and sold as slaves?
visual_treatment: Refinement to the sensitivity rule: default treatment isn't always 'swap in a gentler icon' — sometimes it's no icon at all. This fact gets a plain typographic card with no illustration, since any symbol risks reducing people to a decorative object. Deliberately left without an 'icon' field.

canonical_statement: The American Revolution (Revolutionary War) was fought to win independence from Britain.
linked_questions: What war did the Americans fight to win independence from Britain?
visual_treatment: Reuses the tricorn hat icon (already built for fact 86) — the icon represents the Revolutionary War era generally, not Washington specifically, so reuse across unrelated facts from the same era is intentional.

canonical_statement: Colonists declared independence over taxation without representation, among other reasons.
linked_questions: Name one reason why the Americans declared independence from Britain.
curation_rationale: The most famous and already-quotable phrase of the three — it barely needs an invented mnemonic, since it already functions as a memorable slogan in American civic culture.

canonical_statement: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776.
linked_questions: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
curation_rationale: Only accepted answer. Checked against fact 125 (Independence Day) for overlap since both concern July 4 — kept separate because they test different knowledge: this fact is a specific date-recall question, fact 125 is about what the holiday represents. Borderline, but not the same overlap pattern as 125/126.
visual_treatment: Same burst icon as fact 125 — deliberate reuse since both concern the same date, reinforcing rather than duplicating.

canonical_statement: Five of the 13 original states were New York, New Jersey, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Virginia.
linked_questions: There were 13 original states. Name five.
accepted_answer_variants: Any five of the 13 original states
curated_answer: New York, New Jersey, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Virginia
curation_rationale: Reuses the founder's own proven personal technique (already used in the original deck): three of the thirteen states share the word 'New', which functions as its own memory hook with no external image needed. Massachusetts and Virginia added as two more highly recognizable names to reach five.
visual_treatment: NEW TECHNIQUE, added to the framework: pattern grouping — when several accepted-answer items already share a linguistic or structural pattern, the pattern itself is the mnemonic. No invented imagery needed; the shared prefix is highlighted in the display.

canonical_statement: The U.S. Constitution was written in 1787.
linked_questions: What founding document was written in 1787?
curation_rationale: Only accepted answer. Checked against no other fact currently curated to '1787' as a primary answer — no overlap.
visual_treatment: Icon + date badge combined, same composite pattern as other numeric_badge facts with an icon.
